source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5; 9.6; 20.5

main.t: The long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder to the elbow (humerus).

simpler.t: The humerus is the bone of your upper arm.

deeper.t: It is a long bone: a hollow shaft (diaphysis) with a wider end at each end (epiphysis).

facts.t: It sits in the arm, between the shoulder above and the elbow below.
Its round head faces inwards (medially) and fits the shallow socket of the shoulder blade.
At the elbow it meets the ulna on the inner side and the radius on the outer side.

simpler.t: It runs from your shoulder down to your elbow.

deeper.t: It forms the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint above and part of the elbow joint below.

items.name: Head
items.t: The large, smooth, round top. It forms the shoulder joint with the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

items.name: Anatomical neck
items.t: The edge of the smooth head. It marks where the joint surface ends.

items.name: Greater and lesser tubercles
items.t: Two bumps near the top. The rotator cuff muscles attach to them.

items.name: Intertubercular (bicipital) groove
items.t: The groove between the tubercles. A tendon of biceps brachii runs in it.

items.name: Surgical neck
items.t: Where the wide top narrows into the shaft. It is a common site of fracture.

items.name: Deltoid tuberosity
items.t: A rough V-shaped area halfway down the outer shaft. The deltoid muscle attaches here.

items.name: Medial and lateral epicondyles
items.t: Bony points either side of the elbow. Forearm muscles start from them.

items.name: Trochlea and capitulum
items.t: The pulley-shaped trochlea meets the ulna. The knob-like capitulum meets the radius.

items.name: Olecranon fossa
items.t: A hollow at the back. It takes the tip of the ulna when the elbow straightens.

simpler.t: Its top end makes the shoulder joint and its bottom end makes the elbow joint.

deeper.t: The bone usually breaks at the surgical neck, not the anatomical neck.

facts.t: The big round head sits in a socket about a third of its size. This gives the shoulder its huge range of movement.
The price is stability: the shoulder relies on muscles, not bone, to hold the head in place.
The medial epicondyle is larger than the lateral one. The strong gripping muscles of the forearm pull on it.
Hollows above the elbow surfaces make room for the forearm bones. So the elbow can bend and straighten fully.

simpler.t: Its shape lets the shoulder move freely and the elbow bend and straighten fully.

items.name: Rotator cuff
items.t: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis attach to the tubercles. They hold the head in its socket.

items.name: Deltoid
items.t: Attaches to the deltoid tuberosity on the outer shaft.

items.name: Biceps brachii
items.t: One of its tendons runs in the intertubercular groove.

items.name: Humeral circumflex arteries
items.t: Branches of the axillary artery that supply the area near the head.

items.name: Brachial artery
items.t: Runs down the arm and splits near the elbow into the radial and ulnar arteries.

items.name: Four major nerves
items.t: Four major nerves of the upper limb lie close to the humerus. Fractures can damage them.

items.name: Radial nerve
items.t: Lies in the radial (spiral) groove on the back of the shaft.

simpler.t: Muscles that move the shoulder attach near the top. Important nerves and arteries run close to the bone.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification), like all limb bones except the clavicle.
Bone first appears in the shaft by about the twelfth week. Centres in the ends appear later, usually after birth.
Growth plates between the shaft and ends let the bone lengthen. They close at adult size.
A few people have a small hook of bone above the medial epicondyle (supracondylar process). It can press on the median nerve.

items.injury: A fall onto the hand or elbow breaks the bone across the surgical neck.
items.damaged: The surgical neck; the shaft can be driven into the head (impacted fracture).
items.why: The narrow neck is where the wide top meets the shaft, so force concentrates there.

items.injury: A fracture of the middle of the shaft.
items.damaged: The radial nerve in the radial groove.
items.cannotDo: Lift the wrist and fingers (wrist drop).
items.why: The radial nerve supplies the muscles on the back of the forearm that extend the wrist and fingers.

items.injury: A child falls onto the tip of the elbow and breaks the bone just above the epicondyles (supracondylar fracture).
items.damaged: The artery to the forearm (brachial artery), squeezed by swelling.
items.cannotDo: Keep the forearm muscles healthy: without blood they can quickly be damaged for good.
items.why: The brachial artery runs down to the elbow right beside the broken bone.

items.injury: A fall onto the hand or elbow with the arm raised fully out to the side.
items.damaged: The shoulder joint: the head of the humerus dislocates downwards.
items.why: Muscles and ligaments strongly support the head in front, above and behind, so it comes out downwards.

items.q: Predict the deficit if the radial nerve is damaged in the radial (spiral) groove, and explain why.
model: Wrist drop: the patient cannot lift (extend) the wrist.
The fingers cannot be straightened at the knuckles.
The radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles on the back of the forearm.
Triceps is usually spared: its branches leave the nerve above the groove.
Numbness over the back of the hand near the thumb.

items.q: Explain why most dislocations of the shoulder are downward (inferior).
model: The glenoid cavity is small and shallow: about a third of the size of the head.
Muscles and ligaments support the head in front, above and behind.
The underside has the least support.
Force on a fully raised arm drives the head out downwards.

items.q: Compare the anatomical neck and the surgical neck of the humerus.
model: Anatomical neck: the edge of the smooth joint surface of the head.
Surgical neck: where the wide top joins the narrow shaft.
The surgical neck is a common fracture site.
Fractures there can be impacted, with the shaft driven into the head.

check.stem: Which part of the humerus meets the radius at the elbow?
check.why: The knob-like capitulum meets the radius; the pulley-shaped trochlea meets the ulna.

check.stem: Where does the deltoid muscle attach to the humerus?
check.why: The deltoid tuberosity is the rough V-shaped area halfway down the outer shaft.

check.stem: Why is the medial epicondyle larger than the lateral epicondyle?
options: It bears the weight of the forearm
The strong gripping muscles of the forearm pull on it
It forms the elbow joint with the ulna
check.why: The powerful gripping muscles of the front of the forearm start from it, so it is larger and stronger.
